analysis: The closest option has substantial comparative politics, political thought, international relations, EU institutions and public-policy study. Modern history, law, social theory and sustainability governance add specific disciplinary depth. Replaced general creative writing and one rhetoric course with modern history and public policy to strengthen the target response.

The international option prioritises empire, war, conflict, law, youth radicalisation and governance. Criminal justice adds a bounded legal perspective on security; it is not presented as international-relations theory. The policy/economy option has sustained economics, econometrics, data and institutional content and now includes actual policy analysis. Removed its unavailable criminal-law selection and rescheduled introductory economics.

Every substantive course contribution was reconsidered against the active profile or official description. In particular, the description-only policy course receives full consideration for policy processes and memo work; the history-research course supplies source criticism and a paper, not an assumed current-US-politics survey. Fourteen bounded primary matches replace the original blanket unmatched decision. Broad academic skills, duplicated research roles, specialist current-politics/backsliding seminars, thesis and open choice retain justified blanks.

All three twenty-four-course schedules satisfy offerings, earlier formal prerequisites, Year-1 PPD and the advanced-course minimum. Relevant political, sociological and data foundations precede advanced work where feasible. Each pair passes the numerical and substantive distinctness tests. Optional research remains outside scheduled credits.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: Academic writing, literature evaluation, civic collaboration and reflective practice provide the first-year common foundation.

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.contribution: introduces economic reasoning about markets, resources and government as a foundation for political-economic analysis

BENECON211.name: International Macroeconomics
BENECON211.contribution: examines open-economy macroeconomic dynamics, goods, financial and labour markets, inflation, growth, and fiscal and monetary policy using formal models

BENECON212.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
BENECON212.contribution: examines microeconomic decisions, incentives and behavioural responses, supporting analysis of policy effects and political-economic choices

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.contribution: examines public intervention, equity, public goods, taxation, education, health and social insurance through policy models and research

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.contribution: develops econometric estimation, statistical tests and an empirical paper for analysing causal and predictive economic relationships relevant to policy

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.contribution: develops empirical design, measurement, sampling, statistics and a complete student data-collection project as research foundations for political inquiry

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.contribution: develops data cleaning, transformation, visualisation and applied research in R, supporting empirical investigation of political evidence

DISDATA211.name: Machine Learning
DISDATA211.contribution: develops statistical prediction, regression, classification, model evaluation and data analysis as computational complements to political research

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.contribution: examines institutions, power, participation, justice and collective decision-making in sustainability governance, including a policy-advice or evaluation project

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.contribution: introduces legal traditions, social justice and legal reasoning as foundations for studying political institutions and public power

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.contribution: examines modern political, economic and cultural transformations from 1815 onward through historical sources and inquiry

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.contribution: compares ancient and modern empires through legitimacy, institutions and cultural power, providing historical depth for international politics

GOSHIST213.name: Ways of War
GOSHIST213.contribution: examines warfare, strategy and political power from antiquity onward through historical sources and critical comparison

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.contribution: develops research questions, source criticism and a substantial historical research paper in the American context; its contribution is historical inquiry rather than a current US-politics survey

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.contribution: examines human-rights law and philosophical claims, dignity, international protection and legal-political arguments

GOSLAWJ211.name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
GOSLAWJ211.contribution: examines criminal liability, punishment, criminalisation and justice through legal cases and a criminology or organised-crime research proposal; it adds a legal perspective on security rather than replacing international-relations theory

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.contribution: examines international legal sources, states and institutions, force, conflict, human rights, economic and environmental law, and the political dimensions of law

GOSLAWJ213.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
GOSLAWJ213.contribution: compares constitutions, legislatures, executives, courts, judicial review, rights and administrative remedies as structures of public power

GOSLAWJ312.name: Foundations of European Union Law
GOSLAWJ312.contribution: examines EU institutions, competences, supremacy, citizenship, free movement and judicial remedies through legal cases

GOSPHIL111.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
GOSPHIL111.contribution: develops interpretation and evaluation of philosophical arguments about ethics, knowledge, freedom and identity as foundations for normative political thought

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.contribution: develops moral reasoning and independent ethical arguments relevant to public responsibilities and competing political values

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.contribution: examines historical and contemporary political thought, authority, rights and society through original texts and normative argument

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.contribution: examines democracy, autocratisation, institutions, participation and political behaviour through empirical comparison and a research memo

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.contribution: examines competing international-relations theories, geopolitics, conflicts and global cooperation through case research and a UN simulation

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.contribution: examines EU institutions, integration, representation, legitimacy and policymaking, with an empirical research project on parliamentary amendments and interest influence

GOSPOLI312.name: Public Policy Analysis
GOSPOLI312.contribution: examines policy-making phases, policy actors and alternative analytical frameworks through a sugar-policy case and policy memos

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.contribution: examines conflict, inequality, identity and colonial legacies through interdisciplinary approaches to security, peacebuilding and justice, including a policy brief

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.contribution: examines social identities, institutions, boundaries and inequality as contexts for political participation and power

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: develops qualitative interviewing, documentary inquiry, interpretation and reflexivity for social and political research

GOSSOCI214.name: Modern Sociology
GOSSOCI214.contribution: examines competing modern social theories of power, inequality and cultural difference through critical reading and an empirical case paper

GOSSOCI215.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
GOSSOCI215.contribution: examines social movements, environmental justice and collective action through feminist, anticolonial and other perspectives

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.contribution: examines civil society, trust, solidarity, hegemony and social repair through theory and research on an organisation or initiative

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.contribution: examines social influence, group processes, prejudice, aggression and prosocial behaviour as psychological foundations for political interaction

HCBPSYC315.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism
HCBPSYC315.contribution: examines youth radicalisation, risk, belonging, inclusive education and prevention through research-based teacher resources and a youth toolkit

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.contribution: develops rhetorical argument, audience awareness and public communication as complementary foundations for political debate

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.contribution: examines persuasion, framing and ethical communication through community projects, supporting critical analysis of public communication

alignment.rationale: Both examine government policy in relation to economic organisation and distribution. UvA also studies the history and institutional foundations of capitalism and political-economic theory; UCR concentrates on public intervention and spending.
Both develop research design, evidence evaluation, measurement and empirical analysis. UCR includes a student research project in a broader disciplinary setting.
Both examine sustainability transitions through power, institutions, inclusion, collective action and governance frameworks.
Both study the historical development of modern political, economic and social systems. UCR starts in 1815 rather than 1750.
Both develop an independent academic research question, source work and a substantial scholarly paper. UCR uses historical rather than specifically political-science inquiry.
Both examine constitutional and administrative institutions, rights and legal constraints on public power. UvA situates these in an integrated law-and-politics introduction.
Both examine the history of political ideas through primary texts and relate them to political problems.
Both compare democratic and authoritarian institutions, transitions, political actors and explanations of regime change.
Both develop international-relations theories and apply them to global political problems.
Both develop a political research design, collect or code evidence and analyse and communicate findings. UCR uses an EU parliamentary project; UvA offers broader supervised research themes.
Both examine public policy, actors, policy processes and frameworks for analysing collective responses to social problems.

Both examine international power, conflict, colonial legacies, inequality and security. UvA is a broader advanced survey of International Relations; UCR concentrates on conflict and peace through several disciplines.
Both develop empirical inquiry and methodological judgement. UCR specialises in qualitative methods; UvA also includes quantitative and inferential statistical methods.
Both analyse power, inequality, social categories and difference through competing theoretical perspectives. UvA gives a specifically political and intersectional focus.
No additional selected course directly reproduces the dedicated political-science academic-skills sequence.
Selected political courses address parts of this broad introduction, but their strongest placements are political thought, international relations and comparative regimes. They are not counted twice.
UCR research and political projects are placed with methods and the later research project; no additional course is counted as the distinct first-year project.
No additional selected course directly reproduces the dedicated political-science academic-skills sequence.
No additional selected course directly centres the seminar’s current American-politics and international-connections focus.
Comparative Politics already supplies its strongest primary relationship with the compulsory regimes course. No second course is counted for the specialist backsliding seminar.
No compulsory individual political-science thesis is scheduled at UCR. Optional research is shown separately outside scheduled credits.
Open choice space remains unspecified; no elective, minor or placement is invented.
